Swamp sparrow (Melospiza georgiana) eggs that are incubated at a constant 36 °C [T = 36 °C] typically hatch after approximately 13.25 days [ab = approximately 13.25 days], a duration that falls within the broader range of 12 to 15 days reported for this species under field conditions. Hatchlings emerge with an initial wet body mass of 2.22 grams [Ww0 = 2.22 grams], a modest starting weight that reflects the altricial state of development characteristic of emberizid nestlings, which require extensive parental brooding and provisioning. The yolk-dependent embryo relies entirely on endogenous reserves during the incubation period, and the timing of this trophic switch to exogenous feeding at hatching is a critical developmental milestone. Brooding adults maintain a stable nest microclimate throughout this period, and the thermal conditions of 36 °C [T = 36 °C] appear to be near optimal for synchronizing organogenesis with the depletion of yolk nutrients, ensuring that the altricial nestling emerges with sufficient energy reserves to initiate begging behavior.

Under the thermoneutral conditions typical of active physiological measurement for this species, approximately 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], the basal metabolic rate of adult Swamp sparrows reaches 38 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 38 milliliters of oxygen per hour]. This value was obtained from respirometry trials conducted on resting, post-absorptive individuals and reflects the basal metabolic demands of a bird of this body size. The measurement is consistent with metabolic expectations for emberizids, as the relatively high mass-specific oxygen consumption is linked to the active foraging strategy and high rates of daily energy expenditure that characterize this wetland-obligate passerine. The physiological demands of meeting these basic metabolic needs are especially pronounced during the breeding season, when individuals must balance the energetic costs of thermoregulation with the added metabolic burden of reproductive activity. This basal oxygen consumption rate provides a useful baseline for understanding the species' overall energy budget.

Female Swamp sparrows reach an ultimate wet body mass of 13.9 grams [Wwi = 13.9 grams] at adulthood, a size that represents the asymptotic body mass attained after the completion of somatic growth. This adult body mass is consistent with the typical range for small-bodied emberizids that inhabit freshwater marshes and shrubby wetlands across eastern North America. The relatively modest adult mass constrains the species' life-history strategy, as it limits the volume of the incubating egg and the total energetic reserves available to a provisioning adult during the nestling stage. The trajectory from a hatchling mass of 2.22 grams [Ww0 = 2.22 grams] to this adult mass involves a period of rapid mass gain during the nestling phase, followed by a gradual approach to the asymptotic mass during the juvenile stage. This growth pattern is typical of passerine birds that rely heavily on biparental care to fuel the accelerated growth phase of the developing chick.

A Swamp sparrow female typically lays a single clutch each year [F_R_i = a single clutch each year], containing 3 to 6 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = containing 3 to 6 eggs per clutch], representing a modest annual reproductive output of 3 to 6 eggs per year [Ri = 3 to 6 eggs per year]. Clutch size varies with latitude and habitat quality, with smaller clutches more common in northern populations where the breeding season is shorter. After the eggs hatch, the altricial nestlings are brooded intensively by the female and provisioned by both parents until they reach independence. The period of parental provisioning continues after the juvenile bird leaves the nest, as the fledgling remains dependent on adults for food while learning to forage independently. The relatively low annual fecundity of this species is offset by a high rate of nestling survival under favorable conditions, although nest predation by marsh-dwelling snakes and raccoons can substantially reduce reproductive success in some years. Under the standard thermal conditions of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], the maximum reproductive rate is expressed as a single annual event.

During development under 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], fledging occurs 12.5 days after hatching [tx = 12.5 days after hatching], marking the moment when the young bird achieves its first flight and departs from the nest. This relatively brief nestling period is characteristic of open-cup nesting passerines vulnerable to predation, where selection favors rapid feather development and early departure from the exposed nest site. Following fledging, the immature individual undergoes a period of post-fledging dispersal before reaching puberty at 37.5 days after hatching [tp = 37.5 days after hatching], the stage at which gonadal maturation is first completed at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. First successful reproduction, however, is deferred until 365 days after hatching [tR = 365 days after hatching], or roughly one year of age, as the young bird must acquire a territory and attract a mate during its first spring at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. The maximum lifespan of Swamp sparrow has been documented at 8.6 years [am = 8.6 years] at 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C] based on recapture data from long-term banding studies, a longevity that is comparatively high for a small passerine and reflects the relatively low extrinsic mortality of stable marsh habitats.
